name: changedetection.io
description: Self-hosted web page change detection and notification service with CSS/XPath/JSON selectors, text and visual diffing, optional real-browser fetching, and over 85 notification targets. The same codebase also backs a paid hosted subscription that funds development.
journalism_use_case: Watch specific regions of agency pages, FOIA logs, press-release indexes or policy PDFs and get an email/Slack/Discord alert with a diff when the wording quietly changes.
language_stack: Python (Flask); Docker images; optional Playwright/Puppeteer/Selenium browser fetchers
deployment: self-hosted (pip or Docker/docker-compose); vendor-hosted SaaS also offered
activity_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-16: pushed_at 2026-11-16T08:48:22Z, 35,839 stars, not archived; latest release 0.70.3 published 2026-11-09; HEAD commits dated 2026-11-16 ('Logs - Keep notification URL passwords and the browser token out of the log output', #4741)
platform_api_risk: Low for core HTTP fetching; the browser-based fetchers track fast-moving Chromium/Playwright/Puppeteer releases, and notification delivery depends on third-party services (Apprise targets, SMTP).
external_deps: Apprise for notifications; optional Playwright/Puppeteer/Selenium + Chromium container for JS-heavy pages; Docker
data_flows: Snapshots and diffs stored locally in the self-hosted instance; notification payloads (which can include page text) are sent out to whichever third-party channel is configured.
limitations: Per-URL watch model with no built-in editorial triage/annotation workflow; JS-heavy or bot-protected government portals need the browser fetcher and may still block; frequent releases mean upgrade churn.

name: urlwatch
description: Long-running command-line tool that watches URLs (and shell command output) defined in a YAML jobs file, applies filters to strip boilerplate, and reports unified diffs through pluggable reporters. It is the ancestor of several later monitoring tools.
journalism_use_case: Script a reproducible watchlist of statute, regulation or guidance pages in version control, and receive diffs by email, Slack, Matrix or stdout when an official page is edited.
deployment: self-hosted / local CLI, usually driven by cron or systemd timers
activity_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-16: pushed_at 2026-07-10T08:56:34Z, 3,148 stars, 85 open issues, not archived; HEAD commits dated 2026-07-09/10 ('Browser jobs: Handle HTTP error responses like url jobs', #868). The releases/latest API endpoint returned 404, so release cadence was not confirmed from GitHub releases.
platform_api_risk: Low; plain HTTP fetching plus optional Playwright 'browser' jobs, so JS rendering depends on the browser stack rather than any vendor API.
external_deps: Python 3; optional Playwright for browser jobs; optional jq/html2text/beautifulsoup-style filters; reporter-specific credentials
data_flows: Snapshot cache and diffs stay on the local machine; only the configured reporter transmits content off-box.
limitations: CLI/text-first with no web UI or multi-user triage; no built-in archiving of the captured snapshot as evidence; four-month gap since last push at time of checking.

name: webchanges
description: Actively maintained Python tool, derived from urlwatch, that checks web content (including PDFs, images and command output) for changes and reports rich HTML diffs, with optional AI-generated change summaries. Its licence file notes it redistributes urlwatch 2.21 source under the original BSD terms.
journalism_use_case: Monitor official documents and dashboards that urlwatch handles poorly (PDF text, images, JSON APIs) and receive readable HTML diffs of what an agency altered.
deployment: self-hosted / local CLI via pip, scheduled by cron or Task Scheduler
activity_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-16: pushed_at 2026-11-15T08:26:43Z, 50 stars, 6 open issues, not archived. LICENSE.md read 2026-11-16 states 'The MIT License (MIT) Copyright (c) 2020- Mike Borsetti' plus a redistribution notice for urlwatch release 2.21 under BSD-3-Clause terms.
platform_api_risk: Optional AI summarisation sends page content to an external LLM provider, which is a configuration-time choice; otherwise plain HTTP plus optional Playwright.
external_deps: Python 3; optional Playwright/Chromium; optional LLM API key for AI summaries; reporter credentials
data_flows: Snapshots and diffs held locally; content leaves the machine only via configured reporters or, if enabled, the AI summarisation provider.
limitations: Effectively a single-maintainer project with a small user base; no web UI or collaborative review; AI summary feature introduces a third-party data-sharing decision that newsrooms should review before use on sensitive beats.

name: Klaxon (self-hosted, The Marshall Project)
description: Rails web app, built and used in The Marshall Project newsroom, that lets non-technical reporters 'bookmark' a selected portion of a page with a bookmarklet and be emailed (or Slack/Discord-notified) when that section changes. Its README states the original self-hosted version remains free and open source but is no longer supported for individual users, who are pointed at Klaxon Cloud instead.
journalism_use_case: Give reporters without command-line skills a point-and-click way to watch FOIA disclosure logs, court dockets and agency pages and get alerted to newsworthy edits.
language_stack: Ruby on Rails + PostgreSQL (GitHub reports primary language SCSS); Heroku or Docker deployment
deployment: self-hosted; one-click Heroku deploy is the documented path, with Docker and Ubuntu install guides also present
activity_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-16: pushed_at 2026-11-16T10:03:32Z, 683 stars, not archived; latest release v0.7.0 published 2026-03-09. HEAD commits dated 2026-11-11 are dependency bumps (Rails 8.1.4.1, rubocop-rspec_rails), i.e. upkeep rather than feature work. newsklaxon.org fetched 2026-11-16 and live, directing newsrooms to 'Set Up in Your Newsroom' via GitHub.
platform_api_risk: Deployment-platform rather than API risk: the documented path assumes Heroku (README states Heroku's free tier is gone and budgets roughly $10/month plus SendGrid and Postgres add-ons).
external_deps: Heroku (or self-managed Docker/Linux host), PostgreSQL, SendGrid or other SMTP, optional Slack/Discord webhooks
data_flows: Watch list, snapshots and diffs live in the newsroom's own Postgres instance; alert emails route through the configured mail provider.
limitations: README explicitly warns it 'may break unexpectedly' and may miss a change or fail to send mail; individual-user support has been discontinued; recent repo activity is dependency maintenance, not development.

name: Klaxon Cloud (MuckRock/DocumentCloud Add-On)
description: Rebuild of Klaxon as a DocumentCloud Add-On: a Python add-on script runs each check as a DocumentCloud Add-On Run in GitHub Actions, while a separate monorepo holds the browser extension and SvelteKit site used to pick the page region to watch. Per the Klaxon-Cloud README each detected change is backed by an Internet Archive snapshot and a visual diff.
journalism_use_case: Lets a reporter with only a DocumentCloud account monitor web pages for newsworthy edits without running a server, with an Internet Archive snapshot attached as evidence of the before-and-after.
language_stack: Python add-on script; TypeScript/Svelte 5 + Vite extension and SvelteKit site on Cloudflare Workers
deployment: hosted — runs on DocumentCloud's Add-On platform (scheduling and storage are DocumentCloud Add-On Events/Runs executed in GitHub Actions); source is public for inspection or forking
activity_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-16: MuckRock/Klaxon pushed_at 2026-09-10T21:51:47Z, licence BSD-3-Clause, 9 stars, not archived, LICENSE file present in repo root. MuckRock/Klaxon-Cloud pushed_at 2026-08-26T12:41:36Z, TypeScript, 4 stars, not archived, but no LICENSE file in its root listing. The Marshall Project's klaxon README (read 2026-11-16) points new users to the DocumentCloud-hosted Klaxon.
platform_api_risk: High coupling to one platform stack: DocumentCloud accounts and Add-On Events, GitHub Actions as the execution runtime, Cloudflare Workers for the site, Chrome Web Store/Firefox review for the extension, and the Internet Archive save endpoint for snapshots.
external_deps: DocumentCloud (MuckRock), GitHub Actions, Cloudflare Workers, Internet Archive Wayback save, Chrome/Firefox MV3 extension distribution
data_flows: Watch configuration, run history and detected changes live in MuckRock's DocumentCloud infrastructure rather than the newsroom's own servers; snapshots are pushed to the Internet Archive, so monitored URLs become public in the Wayback Machine.
limitations: The front-end monorepo carries no licence file, so reuse rights for the extension/site code are not verified (the add-on script itself is BSD-3-Clause); hosted model means less control over retention and no air-gapped option.

name: EDGI web-monitoring-db
description: Rails HTTP API that stores versions of tracked pages, records diffs between them, and lets analysts annotate and prioritise changes; it is the database tier of EDGI's Website Monitoring ('Scanner') system, paired with web-monitoring-ui for human review. EDGI runs it as the backend of the Federal Environmental Web Tracker.
journalism_use_case: Provides the newsroom-grade pipeline for monitoring thousands of government pages at once, with an annotation workflow so analysts can separate boilerplate churn from substantive policy rewording before it reaches reporters.
language_stack: Ruby on Rails + PostgreSQL; paired React UI (web-monitoring-ui) and Python tooling (web-monitoring-processing)
deployment: self-hosted server stack (API + database + UI + import pipeline); EDGI operates a public instance
activity_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-16: web-monitoring-db pushed_at 2026-11-13T17:49:19Z, GPL-3.0, 24 stars, not archived; HEAD commits 2026-11-10/13 include 'Upgrade Rails to v8.1.4.1' (#1505). Companion repos checked the same day: web-monitoring-ui pushed 2026-11-06T20:28:37Z (GPL-3.0), web-monitoring-processing pushed 2026-11-16T01:59:31Z (GPL-3.0), web-monitoring-ops pushed 2026-11-13T18:10:44Z, and the project-wide web-monitoring docs repo pushed 2026-07-28 (CC-BY-SA-4.0). The older web-monitoring-versionista-scraper repo is flagged archived.
platform_api_risk: Snapshot supply depends on the Internet Archive Wayback Machine (EDGI's public tracker relies on daily IA captures), so IA availability, rate limits and crawl coverage are upstream dependencies.
external_deps: PostgreSQL, Redis/Sidekiq-style job processing, Internet Archive Wayback as a version source, web-monitoring-diff for diffing, web-monitoring-ui for review
data_flows: Page versions, diffs and analyst annotations are held in the operator's own Postgres database; public EDGI instance exposes tracked-change data through its API and tracker site.
limitations: Multi-repo distributed system (db + ui + processing + diff + ops) that needs real engineering and ops capacity; licence is GPL-3.0 (copyleft), which some newsroom legal teams treat as a constraint; it is a monitoring platform, not a turnkey single-reporter alert tool.

name: EDGI web-monitoring-diff
description: Python library plus optional HTTP server providing a suite of diff algorithms tuned for web content — HTML-aware, text, source and link diffs — originally built for EDGI's web monitoring work and since adopted by other organisations. Documentation describes use as a library or as an on-demand diff web service.
journalism_use_case: Produces the side-by-side and inline HTML diffs that let a reporter see exactly which sentences, links or data tables were removed from an official page between two archived captures.
language_stack: Python (Tornado-based diff server); C extension for some diff routines
deployment: library embedded in your own code, or self-hosted HTTP diff service (Docker available)
activity_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-16: pushed_at 2026-11-13T07:33:57Z, GPL-3.0, 26 stars, 47 open issues, not archived. readthedocs.io fetched 2026-11-16 shows release history through version 0.3.0 dated 2026-11-12 and describes library plus optional HTTP-server usage.
platform_api_risk: None directly — it diffs content you supply; risk sits with whatever fetches or archives the captures.
external_deps: Python 3; optional Docker; callers typically pair it with web-monitoring-db or the Wayback Machine for version storage
data_flows: Processes content in memory or over a local HTTP endpoint; no outbound data flows of its own.
limitations: A component rather than a product: no scheduling, storage, alerting or UI; HTML diffing of heavily templated government pages still needs filtering to suppress navigation and timestamp noise; GPL-3.0 copyleft.

name: wayback (Python client for the Internet Archive Wayback Machine)
description: Python API client for the Internet Archive Wayback Machine that searches CDX capture indexes and retrieves the raw archived content of specific mementos, built and maintained by EDGI for its government-website monitoring pipeline.
journalism_use_case: Enumerate every archived capture of a government URL and pull the exact bytes of two dates to prove what a page said before and after an edit, without screen-scraping the Wayback web interface.
deployment: library installed via pip into your own scripts or pipeline
activity_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-16: pushed_at 2026-11-06T21:30:02Z, licence BSD-3-Clause confirmed via the licence endpoint (LICENSE at main), 94 stars, not archived.
platform_api_risk: High dependency on Internet Archive services: the CDX/memento endpoints are undocumented-to-semi-documented, rate limited, occasionally unavailable, and subject to IA's terms and exclusion policies, all of which can break or blank out a monitoring run.
external_deps: Internet Archive Wayback Machine CDX and memento endpoints; Python 3; requests-style HTTP stack
data_flows: Sends the URLs you query to the Internet Archive and pulls archived content back; nothing is published, but your query pattern is visible to IA.
limitations: Only as good as IA's crawl coverage — pages never captured, captured rarely, or excluded cannot be reconstructed; no diffing, scheduling or alerting of its own.

name: Awesome Website Change Monitoring
description: EDGI-maintained inventory of the website diffing and change-monitoring landscape, split into open-source tools and hosted services, with a companion comparison spreadsheet; it explicitly aims to map the whole (small) tool space rather than curate favourites.
journalism_use_case: The fastest way for a newsroom to see what monitoring options exist and which are abandoned before committing engineering time, and it is where commercial alternatives such as Fluxguard/Versionista, VisualPing, Wachete and PageFreezer are catalogued.
activity_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-16: pushed_at 2026-08-11T19:40:32Z, CC0-1.0, 515 stars, not archived. readme.md read 2026-11-16: lists DiffEngine, EDGI Web Monitoring, Huginn, Klaxon, NewsDiffs, NYTdiff, Pagelyzer, Time Machine and Website Change Monitor as open source, plus a hosted-services section.
external_deps: None; the deeper comparison lives in an external Google Spreadsheet linked from the readme
limitations: Several entries are stale or now unmaintained (NewsDiffs, NYTdiff, DiffEngine, Pagelyzer) and the list does not flag that; it omits the generalist tools journalists now often use (urlwatch, webchanges, git-scraping approaches); the comparison spreadsheet is hosted off-platform and its freshness was not verified.

name: ArchiveBox
description: Self-hosted web archiving application that takes URLs from feeds, bookmarks, browser history or the CLI and saves multiple renditions of each page — HTML, screenshot, PDF, WARC, media and more — into a browsable local archive with a web UI.
journalism_use_case: Build your own tamper-evident archive of official pages and documents on a schedule, so that when an agency rewrites or deletes a page you hold dated local copies rather than depending on a third-party archive.
language_stack: Python (Django) with many external extractor binaries; Docker images
deployment: self-hosted via pip, Docker or docker-compose; local web UI plus CLI
activity_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-16: pushed_at 2026-11-16T08:31:07Z, MIT, 29,034 stars, 154 open issues, not archived; latest release v0.9.77 published 2026-10-27; HEAD commits dated 2026-11-16 bumping to 0.9.78rc234, i.e. an active release-candidate train.
platform_api_risk: Moderate and indirect: several extractors wrap third-party tools and services (for example media downloaders and the Internet Archive save endpoint), so extractor-level breakage and site terms-of-service questions follow those dependencies rather than ArchiveBox itself.
external_deps: Chromium/Playwright for screenshots and PDFs, wget, curl, yt-dlp, singlefile, readability and other extractor binaries; SQLite/Django
data_flows: Everything is stored on the operator's own disk by default; optional extractors can submit URLs to the Internet Archive, which makes the monitored URL public.
limitations: Not a change-detection tool — it captures and preserves, and diffing between snapshots is not its job; heavy dependency surface and long-running release-candidate versions; archive size grows quickly with multiple renditions per page.

name: browsertrix-crawler
description: Browser-based archival crawler that runs in a single Docker container and produces high-fidelity WARC/WACZ captures of JavaScript-heavy sites, including behaviours that scroll, expand and play content during capture. It is the crawler engine behind Webrecorder's hosted Browsertrix service.
journalism_use_case: Capture modern government portals, dashboards and interactive document viewers faithfully enough that the archived copy still behaves like the live page when a disputed change is later examined.
language_stack: TypeScript/Node.js driving Chromium (Brave builds); Redis for crawl state; Docker
deployment: self-hosted Docker container (CLI-driven); Webrecorder also runs the hosted Browsertrix platform, whose own source is AGPL-3.0 at webrecorder/browsertrix
activity_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-16: pushed_at 2026-11-14T19:26:24Z, AGPL-3.0, 1,197 stars, 152 open issues, not archived; latest release v1.15.4 published 2026-11-11; HEAD commits 2026-11-10/11 include 'deps: update to brave 1.99' and 'deps: browsertrix-behaviors 0.16.0'. The companion webrecorder/browsertrix repo was pushed 2026-11-14T01:26:58Z (AGPL-3.0).
platform_api_risk: Tracks upstream Chromium/Brave releases closely, and capture of login-walled or bot-protected government systems raises access and terms-of-service questions that are the operator's to resolve.
external_deps: Docker, Chromium/Brave, Redis, browsertrix-behaviors; WACZ replay typically via ReplayWeb.page or pywb
data_flows: WARC/WACZ output is written to storage you control (local disk or S3-compatible); nothing is sent to Webrecorder unless you use the hosted service.
limitations: No change detection or alerting — it is capture infrastructure; AGPL-3.0 has network-service implications if you expose a modified version; resource-hungry (a real browser per worker) and requires ops familiarity with Docker.

name: Scoop
description: Browser-based single-page web archiving library and CLI, described by its maintainers as built for 'witnessing the web' — it captures one page at high fidelity with an emphasis on provenance and verifiable capture records. It comes from the lab behind Perma.cc.
journalism_use_case: Capture a single official page at the moment you read it, with provenance metadata attached, so the capture stands up later as evidence of what the page said before a quiet edit.
language_stack: JavaScript/Node.js with a headless browser; WARC/WACZ output
deployment: self-hosted CLI or embedded as a Node library
activity_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-16: pushed_at 2026-09-25T16:00:00Z, MIT confirmed via licence endpoint (LICENSE at main), 217 stars, not archived. Sibling repo harvard-lil/perma pushed 2026-11-03T17:06:15Z, though its licence was not returned by the GitHub licence metadata.
platform_api_risk: Low; it drives a local browser. Capabilities such as attested/signed captures depend on the surrounding toolchain rather than a vendor API.
external_deps: Node.js, a Chromium-family browser, WARC/WACZ tooling; replay needs ReplayWeb.page or pywb
data_flows: Captures are written locally to files you control; no third-party submission by default.
limitations: Single-page scope by design — no crawling, scheduling, diffing or alerting; detailed capabilities (for example signing and provenance summary formats) were not individually verified here beyond the maintainers' own description.

name: pywb
description: Core Python web archiving toolkit for recording and, above all, replaying web archives — it serves WARC/WACZ collections as a browsable Wayback-style interface and can proxy-record new captures.
journalism_use_case: Stand up a private Wayback Machine over your own captures so editors and lawyers can click through dated versions of a government page side by side without relying on a public archive staying online.
language_stack: Python; WARC/CDXJ indexes; Docker images available
deployment: self-hosted server (wayback CLI / Docker), typically fronting a collection of WARC or WACZ files
activity_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-16: pushed_at 2026-11-16T07:47:24Z, GPL-3.0 confirmed via licence endpoint (LICENSE at main), 1,720 stars, 189 open issues, not archived.
platform_api_risk: None inherent; it replays archives you hold.
external_deps: Python 3; WARC/WACZ inputs from crawlers such as browsertrix-crawler, Heritrix, wget or warcprox
data_flows: Serves local archive files; what it exposes to the network depends entirely on how you deploy it.
limitations: Replay and recording only — no change detection, diffing or alerting; replay fidelity for heavily scripted modern pages remains an open problem in web archiving generally; GPL-3.0 copyleft.

name: shot-scraper
description: CLI that uses Playwright to take scripted screenshots of web pages and to scrape them with JavaScript, driven by a YAML file of shots. It is the capture half of the 'git scraping' pattern, where scheduled runs commit outputs to a Git repository so the commit history becomes the change log.
journalism_use_case: Run a scheduled job that screenshots or extracts a government page and commits the result to Git, turning every quiet edit into a dated, diffable commit you can point at in a story.
language_stack: Python + Playwright/Chromium; YAML shot definitions; pairs with git-history (Apache-2.0) and Datasette (Apache-2.0) for analysis
deployment: local CLI or scheduled CI runner (commonly GitHub Actions on a cron)
activity_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-16: shot-scraper pushed_at 2026-10-14T03:21:49Z, Apache-2.0 confirmed via licence endpoint (LICENSE at main), 2,608 stars, not archived. Companion repos checked the same day: simonw/git-history pushed 2025-12-21T20:22:54Z (Apache-2.0), simonw/datasette pushed 2026-11-16T05:26:57Z (Apache-2.0).
platform_api_risk: Depends on Playwright/Chromium upgrades; if run in CI, on that CI provider's scheduling and runner policies (GitHub Actions cron reliability and usage limits).
external_deps: Python 3, Playwright browsers; optional GitHub Actions or other scheduler; optional git-history/Datasette for querying the resulting history
data_flows: Outputs land in your repository or local disk; if the repo is public, the monitored URLs and captured content become public too.
limitations: No notification or diff-review layer — you assemble alerting yourself from Git tooling or CI; requires comfort with YAML, Git and CI; screenshots alone are not text-diffable, so pair with JS/text extraction.

name: diffengine
maintainer: Documenting the Now (DocNow); originally Ed Summers
description: Tool that watches RSS/Atom feeds for changed story content, saves a snapshot to the Internet Archive when it detects a change, generates a diff image, and pushes it to social media (Twitter or email per its README) while building a local database of diffs. Development appears to have stopped in 2020.
journalism_use_case: The reference design for publicly surfacing stealth edits to anything with a feed — news sites, ministry press-release feeds, agency blogs — with an Internet Archive snapshot attached to each detected change.
language_stack: Python 3; feedparser + readability; GeckoDriver/Selenium for diff images; SQLite-backed local database
deployment: self-hosted CLI run on a schedule against a per-instance config directory
activity_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-16: pushed_at 2020-06-25T17:20:50Z, MIT, 182 stars, 30 open issues, repository not flagged archived; HEAD commit dated 2020-06-25 and latest release v0.2.7 published 2020-09-30 — roughly six years without development at time of checking.
platform_api_risk: Severe. It was written for the pre-2023 Twitter API; free write access to X/Twitter has since been restricted, and the README describes Twitter or email delivery, so social posting should be assumed broken without rework. It also depends on the Internet Archive save endpoint and on GeckoDriver/Selenium versions that have moved on.
external_deps: Twitter API credentials (historically), Internet Archive save endpoint, GeckoDriver/Firefox, feedparser, readability
data_flows: Diffs are stored locally, but the design is deliberately public: snapshots go to the Internet Archive and diff images are posted to a social account, so monitoring activity is visible to the monitored party.
limitations: Unmaintained since 2020 with broken-by-default social integration and aged browser-automation dependencies; only monitors content reachable through a feed, so pages without RSS/Atom are out of scope.

name: NewsDiffs
maintainer: Eric Price, Greg Price, Jennifer 8. Lee and contributors (ecprice)
description: Django website and scraping framework, built at a 2012 Knight-Mozilla MIT hackathon, that tracked silent edits to online news articles using hand-written parser modules per publication and published the diffs at newsdiffs.org. Its README still specifies Python 2.6+ and Django from Debian packages.
journalism_use_case: The canonical prior art for stealth-edit tracking and a useful reference for how to structure per-site parsers and a public diff archive; not a tool to deploy today.
language_stack: Python 2 + Django (per README); per-site parser modules; Git-backed article store
deployment: self-hosted Django site plus scraper cron (as documented in 2012-era instructions)
activity_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-16: 506 stars, 36 open issues, not flagged archived, and pushed_at 2026-04-13T16:51:50Z — but the default-branch HEAD commit is dated 2018-06-16 ('Merge pull request #49') and the releases/latest endpoint returned 404, so the recent push does not reflect default-branch development. LICENSE read 2026-11-16: MIT/Expat text, with a note that some files carry their own licences.
platform_api_risk: Not an API problem but a parser problem: each monitored publication needs a bespoke parser, and the 2012-2018 parsers target long-since-redesigned sites. The Python 2 runtime is itself end-of-life.
external_deps: Python 2.6+, Django (old versions), per-site HTML parsers; newsdiffs.org public instance status not verified
data_flows: Self-hosted; the original project published detected diffs publicly on its own website.
limitations: Effectively abandoned (last default-branch commit 2018) on an end-of-life runtime; README itself notes you must be a programmer to add a parser for each new site; the mixed per-file licensing means reuse needs file-by-file checking.

name: DataIndex.us (Federal Data Terminations Tracker)
description: Hosted tracker monitoring US federal data infrastructure — dataset availability, new releases, and planned and unplanned changes to collections — including a Federal Data Terminations Tracker and daily aggregation of Information Collection Requests. The site footer states GPL v3 for code and CC BY-SA 4.0 for content, but no public code repository was located.
journalism_use_case: Check whether a federal dataset you are about to rely on has been terminated, altered or had variables removed, and pick up story leads from documented removals and pending collection changes.
deployment: vendor-hosted website and newsletter; no self-hosting path found
activity_evidence: dataindex.us fetched 2026-11-16: operated by FAS, lists Take Action, Change Requests (updated daily), Data Checkup and newsletter sections, and states GPL v3 for code and CC BY-SA 4.0 for content. AHCJ blog post dated November 2026 reports 375 tracker entries as of October 2026 (38 terminated data products, 337 data elements removed) and that The Guardian used it to report nearly 400 federal datasets deleted or altered. GitHub searches on 2026-11-16 (repository search and the fas-org organisation listing) surfaced no corresponding public repository.
platform_api_risk: Entirely dependent on FAS continuing to run and fund the service; no API was advertised on the homepage, so programmatic access and bulk export are unconfirmed.
external_deps: FAS infrastructure; upstream federal sources (agency sites, data.gov, Federal Register ICR notices)
data_flows: Journalists read from the hosted site or email newsletter and can report missing data to the team; no local data holding.
limitations: Despite the site's GPL v3 code statement, no public repository was found, so it cannot be verified as open-source software or self-hosted — treat it as a hosted dataset/dashboard; scope is federal data products rather than arbitrary web pages, and there is no per-URL alerting for pages you choose.
